subject: industrial-systems
audience: FE Industrial & Systems candidates and industrial engineering students
title: The Higher-Rate Distribution Center That Cost $10,000 Less
featured_title: THE HIGHER RATE DISTRIBUTION CENTER THAT COST 10000 DOLLARS LESS

presentation.challenge: Site A had the higher simple average freight rate, but most demand was on its low-cost lane. Demand-weighted annual cost made Site A $10,000 cheaper.

practice.primary_question: How should customer demand and lane transportation rates be combined when comparing distribution-center locations?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Averaging lane freight rates without weighting each rate by the shipment volume assigned to that lane.

case_dna.target_misconception: The distribution center with the lower simple average freight rate must have the lower annual transportation cost.
case_dna.why_plausible: Average rate is easy to compare, but it ignores that customer regions can have very different shipment volumes.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: Annual demand is 8000 units West and 2000 East. Site A rates are $2 and $8, yielding $32,000/year. Site B rates are $4 and $5, yielding $42,000/year, even though Site B's simple average lane rate is lower.
case_dna.corrected_model: Compare network alternatives using shipment-volume-weighted transportation cost: total cost=Σ(demand_i×rate_i).

problem_statement: A company must choose one distribution-center site to serve two annual markets: West demand=8,000 units and East demand=2,000 units. Transportation rates from Site A are $2/unit to West and $8/unit to East. Rates from Site B are $4/unit to West and $5/unit to East. Fixed facility costs are equal and may be ignored. A note chooses Site B because its simple average rate, $4.50/unit, is lower than Site A's $5.00/unit. Determine the lower-cost site and annual transportation-cost difference.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The lower average freight rate was not the lower total freight cost.
facts: West demand is four times East demand
Site A is much cheaper to West
Site B has the lower unweighted average lane rate
gates.prompt: What must weight each transportation rate?

options.label: Use total cost=Σ(demand×lane rate)
options.reason: Transportation cost depends on both the rate and the quantity shipped on each lane.

options.label: Compare the simple average of lane rates
options.reason: That assumes equal shipment quantities across lanes.

options.label: Choose whichever site has the single lowest lane rate
options.reason: One lane alone does not represent total network cost.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the lower annual transportation cost
gates.prompt: Enter the lower annual cost in dollars.

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Cost both distribution networks
gates.result: Site A has the lower annual transportation cost at $32,000.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the annual network cost
gates.success: Site A=$32,000/year; Site B=$42,000/year; Site A saves $10,000/year.
gates.hint: Multiply each market's annual demand by its lane-specific rate.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: Shipment volume makes the low-cost West lane decisive

cards.text: Site A saves $10,000/year despite its higher simple average lane rate.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the distribution-network note
report: C1. Site A's simple average lane rate is $5.00/unit.
C2. Site B's simple average lane rate is $4.50/unit.
C3. Therefore Site B has the lower annual transportation cost.

claims.label: C1
claims.reason: The arithmetic mean of Site A's two rates is $5.00.

claims.label: C2
claims.reason: The arithmetic mean of Site B's two rates is $4.50.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: The conclusion ignores unequal customer demand and therefore ignores shipment-volume weighting.

evidence_choices.label: Site A=$32,000 versus Site B=$42,000 per year
evidence_choices.reason: These totals weight each lane rate by the actual annual demand.

correction.template: Site {site} is preferred at ${cost}/year, saving ${savings}/year in transportation cost.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Find when Site B becomes equally costly
gates.constraint: Keep total annual demand at 10,000 units; let West demand be W and East demand be 10,000-W.

options.label: At W=8,000 units
options.reason: At 8,000 West units, Site A is still $10,000 cheaper.

options.label: At W=2,000 units
options.reason: At that mix, Site B is cheaper rather than equal.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply weighted transportation cost
gates.prompt: A site serves 3,000 units at $6/unit and 7,000 units at $2/unit. What is annual transportation cost?

options.label: $40,000/year
options.reason: That incorrectly applies the simple average rate of $4 to all units.

options.label: $80,000/year
options.reason: That adds rates before multiplying by total volume.

gates.explanation: Network transportation cost is a shipment-volume-weighted sum across lanes.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the distribution-network comparison
gates.confirmation: I confirm that transportation alternatives must be evaluated using lane rates weighted by shipment volume, not a simple average of rates.

items.label: What failed
items.value: Lane freight rates were averaged without considering customer demand.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: Most annual volume moved on the West lane, where Site A had the major cost advantage.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use total annual transport cost Σ(demand×rate).

seo.seo_title: Weighted Transportation Cost and Network Selection | FE E-086
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Industrial & Systems Case E-086: demand-weighted freight costs make Site A $32,000/year versus $42,000 for Site B.
seo.focus_keyphrase: FE Industrial weighted transportation cost network
seo.excerpt: A lower average freight rate does not guarantee a lower network cost when customer demand differs by lane.
seo.direct_answer: Site A costs 8000($2)+2000($8)=$32,000/year. Site B costs 8000($4)+2000($5)=$42,000/year. Site A is therefore $10,000/year cheaper.

faqs.q: How should transportation rates be compared across unequal markets?
faqs.a: Weight each lane rate by the shipment quantity or demand on that lane.

faqs.q: When would the two sites in this case have equal transport cost?
faqs.a: When West and East demand are each 5,000 units per year.
